articles.title: Commercially available AI medical devices for prostate MRI: current evidence and opportunities for implementation.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Artificial intelligence (AI) may improve prostate MRI interpretation and reduce radiologist workload, but evidence supporting clinical implementation remains limited. This scoping review summarises evidence on commercially available AI medical devices for prostate MRI. MATERIALS AND METHODS: PubMed was searched for studies published through October 1, 2026. Eligible devices were cleared by the United States Food and Drug Administration and/or CE marked, with commercial availability corroborated through manufacturer websites. Data extraction addressed standalone AI performance, AI-assisted radiologist performance, workflow efficiency, and downstream clinical impact. RESULTS: Twenty-one studies evaluating 7 commercial AI systems were included; 17/21 (81%) were retrospective and 14/21 (67%) were single-centre. AI assistance suggested greater benefit for less-experienced readers, but improvements were inconsistent and increased specificity sometimes accompanied reduced sensitivity. Standalone evaluations, outside the devices' approved intended use, showed discrimination comparable to that of radiologists in selected cohorts. Inter-reader agreement and workflow benefits were mixed. We identify three key limitations of the current body of evidence that require thoughtful consideration before routine implementation: (1) incomplete verification strategies, (2) limited determination of workflow benefit, and (3) lack of analyses of cost-effectiveness and patient outcomes, e.g., time to treat or cancer-free survival. CONCLUSION: Evidence supporting the use of commercial AI for prostate MRI remains limited and heterogeneous, with inconsistent diagnostic benefits. Prospective comparative studies in real clinical workflows are needed to determine its potential role within the prostate cancer diagnostic pathway. KEY POINTS: Question Evidence for clinical implementation of prostate AI remains limited-most studies are retrospective and single-centre, with heterogeneous populations and reference standards. Findings AI may improve diagnostic performance for less-experienced readers, but gains for expert readers and assessment of workflow efficiency are limited. Clinical relevance Prospective multicentre studies embedded in real-world pathways are needed, together with analyses of cost-effectiveness and patient outcomes.

articles.title: (Elastography) E-BI-RADS: A Novel Classification System for Breast Elastography to Enable Safe Biopsy De-escalation.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Determining the probability of malignancy of a breast lesion allows for the appropriate triage of follow-up. Although BI-RADS provides standardized risk stratification for mammography, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging, no equivalent classification system exists for breast elastography. The aim of this study was to develop and evaluate a data-driven E-BI-RADS classification for breast elastography and to compare its diagnostic performance with B-mode BI-RADS. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective study, consecutive patients undergoing breast imaging with available B-mode ultrasound, shear-wave elastography (SWE), and strain elastography (10L4 transducer, Siemens ACUSON Sequoia) from 06/2023 to 12/2025 were included. A multivariable logistic regression model combining SWE velocity and elastography-to-B-mode lesion size (E/B) ratio was used to estimate malignancy probability, followed by Platt recalibration. Data-driven probability cutoffs were derived to define E-BI-RADS categories aligned with the BI-RADS concept. (E-)BI-RADS categories 4 and 5 were considered an indication for biopsy. Histopathologic evaluation or imaging follow-up served as the reference standard. RESULTS: The cohort comprised 344 breast lesions in 337 patients, including 224 (65.1%) malignant and 120 (34.9%) benign lesions. B-mode BI-RADS achieved a sensitivity of 98.6% (221/224) and a specificity of 34.2% (41/120). E-BI-RADS demonstrated malignancy rates of 0.0% in E-BI-RADS 2 (0/71); 5.3% in E-BI-RADS 3 (1/19); 85.2% in E-BI-RADS 4 (155/182); and 94.4% in E-BI-RADS 5 (68/70). E-BI-RADS achieved a sensitivity of 99.6% (223/224) and a specificity of 74.2% (89/120). The single false-negative case was a 31 mm B-cell lymphoma, classified as E-BI-RADS 3, with a shear-wave velocity of 4.4 m/s and an E/B ratio of 0.9. Decision-curve analysis demonstrates that E-BI-RADS achieves higher net benefit than SWE-based and B-mode BI-RADS strategies. DISCUSSION: E-BI-RADS provides the first standardized, BI-RADS-like classification system for breast elastography and enables safe biopsy de-escalation with excellent sensitivity and improved specificity compared with existing approaches.

articles.title: The COSAS 2024 challenge: Cross-Organ and Cross-Scanner Adenocarcinoma Segmentation for domain generalization in computational pathology.
articles.abstract: Histopathological assessment remains the gold standard for cancer diagnosis. However, automated histopathology models can be sensitive to domain shifts arising from organ-specific morphological heterogeneity and scanner-associated acquisition variability. To investigate these complementary sources of variation, we established the Cross-Organ and Cross-Scanner Adenocarcinoma Segmentation (COSAS) 2024 Challenge, comprising separate cross-organ and cross-scanner segmentation tasks. The benchmark includes 580 pixel-level annotated histopathology patches spanning six organ sites and six scanner platforms. Thirty international teams submitted valid solutions using a range of convolutional, transformer-based, and hybrid architectures together with different training, augmentation, and inference strategies. Separately, we evaluated conventional segmentation networks and foundation-model-based baselines as organizer-run references. Performance varied substantially across domains and between the two tasks. The relative strengths of the reference models were task dependent, with no model family uniformly strongest across both settings, while the leading challenge submissions achieved competitive performance through different combinations of augmentation, multi-domain training, model design, and inference-time refinement. Overall, COSAS provides a controlled benchmark for studying cross-domain adenocarcinoma segmentation and offers practical insights into the design of AI systems that can better handle the biological and technical variability encountered in diagnostic workflows.

articles.title: Memory-guided mutual information optimization in retinal imaging for early stroke detection and subtyping.
articles.abstract: Effective stroke prevention relies on identifying at-risk individuals before neurological symptoms arise, yet this is severely limited by the absence of scalable screening tools. To address this, we developed RetCEVD, a diagnostic framework that uses rapid, non-invasive retinal Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography (OCTA) for auxiliary assessment of ICVD. At its core, RetCEVD introduces a memory-guided mutual information optimization strategy that maximizes shared disease-relevant information within the same diagnostic category while suppressing redundant or confounding dependencies across different categories. This dual information constraint encourages compact, discriminative representations of subtle retinal microvascular abnormalities. Trained and validated on a multi-center cohort of 24,438 retinal images, RetCEVD addresses three primary tasks: auxiliary detection of existing ICVD, etiological subtyping (large artery atherosclerosis vs. small vessel disease), and current symptomatic-status classification (asymptomatic vs. symptomatic LAA). The model achieved AUCs of 0.95 internal and 0.94 external for ICVD detection, 0.83 internal and 0.81 external for etiological subtyping, and 0.75 internal and 0.76 external for current symptomatic-status classification. The two-year ALAA follow-up provided supplementary longitudinal validation for subsequent stroke events (AUC, 0.71). By comprehensively evaluating the model's clinical interpretability, including its learned pathological features and alignment with established clinical patterns, we provide novel insights into retina-based stroke evaluation. Ultimately, RetCEVD may serve as an efficient, low-cost screening and triage tool to identify individuals who may benefit from confirmatory neurovascular imaging and specialist assessment.

articles.title: Comprehensive multi-organ and body composition phenotyping identifies metabolic signatures associated with incident type 2 diabetes.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To derive a multi-organ imaging biomarker panel from whole-body MRI and evaluate its predictive value for incident type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), including the role of intermuscular adipose tissue (IMAT) in reconciling discrepancies between muscle volume and metabolic risk. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective cohort study analyzed 46,129 UK Biobank participants without diabetes at the time of imaging. Organ volume indices and fat fractions were extracted from Dixon MRI through automated segmentation. Associations between muscle volume indices, fat fractions, and handgrip strength were evaluated, and IMAT was graded in strength-matched participants. Independent imaging biomarkers were identified using adjusted Cox models, and a deep learning model was trained. Added value relative to the Leicester risk assessment score was evaluated using decision curve analysis. RESULTS: During follow-up, 600 participants developed T2DM. Eight biomarkers independently predicted incident T2DM, including liver volume index (hazard ratio (HR), 1.28; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.19-1.38), pancreas fat fraction (HR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.10-1.28), and gluteus fat fraction (HR, 1.17; 95% CI, 1.08-1.27). Gluteal IMAT grades were higher in weak-for-volume participants than in strength-matched controls (median, 2.0 vs 1.0; p = 0.02). The deep learning model achieved a concordance index of 0.814 (95% CI, 0.797-0.832) and, when applied sequentially with clinical criteria, reduced false-positive classifications by 43.0% while preserving 97.3% of true positives. CONCLUSION: Whole-body MRI-derived multi-organ biomarkers independently predicted incident T2DM and enhanced risk stratification beyond an established clinical risk score. Muscle fat fraction may better reflect metabolic risk than muscle volume in IMAT-rich regions. KEY POINTS: Question Clinical risk scores miss the multi-organ pathophysiology of type 2 diabetes; does whole-body MRI organ size and fat quantification improve prediction of incident diabetes? Findings Eight MRI-derived biomarkers independently predicted incident type 2 diabetes; a deep learning model using whole-body MRI biomarkers reached a concordance index of 0.814. Clinical relevance Automated whole-body MRI biomarkers capture multi-organ metabolic signatures beyond conventional risk scoring. Applied after clinical screening, they remove 43.0% of false-positive classifications while preserving 97.3% of true positives.

articles.title: Evaluation of a Rapid and Practical Deep Learning Framework for T1-weighted MRI-based Brain Age Estimation.
articles.abstract: Purpose To develop and evaluate a rapid brain-age estimation framework using freely available Python tools and assess the clinical relevance of brain-age gap (BAG). Materials and Methods In this retrospective study conducted from March 2025 to August 2026, T1-weighted MR images from cohorts of cognitively normal adults (n = 4,346) were divided into training, validation, and internal test sets; two cohorts (n = 315 and 209) served as external test sets. Clinical evaluation used the BICWALZS cohort (n = 954; cognitively normal and various dementias). Preprocessing used freely available Python tools only. The model was trained to predict chronological age as the reference standard. Associations of the residualized BAG with diagnosis, amyloid PET positivity, white matter hyperintensity (WMH) severity, stroke history, and longitudinal clinical worsening were evaluated using ANCOVA, logistic regression, and Cox models. Results The development cohort included 4,346 cognitively normal adults (mean age, 47.0 ± 21.2 years; 2,414 women). Chronological age prediction yielded R2 = 0.95 and MAE, 3.76 years in the internal test set and R2 = 0.69-0.90 and MAE, 4.82-5.15 years in external test sets. The residualized BAG increased across diagnostic groups (P < .001) and was associated with WMH severity (odds ratio [OR], 1.64; P < .001) and stroke history (OR, 1.46; P < .001), but not with amyloid positivity after full adjustment (P = .17), and predicted longitudinal clinical worsening (HR, 1.92). Conclusion The framework accurately predicted age, while residualized BAG was associated with diagnosis, cerebrovascular burden, and longitudinal clinical worsening. © RSNA, 2026.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence in Orthopedic Image Analysis: A Systematic Review and Unified Taxonomy of Bone Age Assessment and Fracture Detection.
articles.abstract: Bone age assessment (BAA) and fracture detection are essential tasks in orthopedic radiography, since they aid diagnosis and clinical decision-making in trauma treatment. Recent technologies in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL), have enhanced the ability to analyze radiological images with greater accuracy and consistency. However, current studies are incomplete, with inconsistent evaluation methodologies, limited external validation, and insufficient interpretability, limiting clinical implementation. This study provides a systematic PRISMA-based review of 116 studies (2017-2025) that analyze imaging modalities, datasets, model architectures, evaluation techniques, and clinical relevance. A uniform taxonomy is introduced to define techniques based on task, modality, and learning paradigm, along with a comparative methodology to address inconsistencies across studies. The findings indicate that CNN and transformer-based models achieve MAE as low as 0.4-0.7 years and accuracy exceeding 95% in controlled datasets but are limited by dataset bias, poor generalization, and a lack of standardized benchmarks. Although explainable AI (XAI) approaches increase interpretability, their clinical reliability is still limited. This review synthesizes current methodologies, identifies key problems, and proposes future directions for AI systems that are robust, interpretable, and clinically deployable, while unifying BAA and fracture detection under a single taxonomy that integrates modality, task, and learning paradigm.

T1 mapping-based heterogeneity analysis of Gd-EOB-DTPA-enhanced MRI in cirrhotic nodules: biological basis, emerging evidence, and future perspectives.
articles.abstract: Liver cirrhosis is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and accurate risk stratification of cirrhotic nodules remains a clinical challenge. During hepatocarcinogenesis, regenerative and dysplastic nodules undergo heterogeneous alterations in hepatocyte function, transporter expression, vascular architecture, and tissue composition. However, conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment of intranodular signal heterogeneity largely relies on subjective visual interpretation and lacks standardized and reproducible quantitative biomarkers. Gadoxetic acid disodium (Gd-EOB-DTPA)-enhanced MRI provides functional information during the hepatobiliary phase by reflecting hepatocyte-specific uptake mediated by organic anion transporting polypeptides. Impaired transporter expression during malignant transformation is associated with reduced contrast uptake and may contribute to spatially heterogeneous contrast distribution. Quantitative T1 mapping enables voxel-wise measurement of absolute T1 relaxation times, thereby providing an objective and quantitative approach to tissue characterization. However, most existing studies have primarily focused on mean T1 values or global reduction rates, while intranodular spatial heterogeneity remains insufficiently explored. MRI-based heterogeneity analysis may complement conventional mean-value analysis by capturing regional variations within lesions. However, direct evidence on T1 mapping-derived heterogeneity in cirrhotic nodules remains limited, and its incremental value over mean T1 values for reflecting hepatocellular function or early malignant transformation has not been established. Quantitative heterogeneity descriptors, including standard deviation, coefficient of variation, histogram-based parameters, and texture features, can objectively characterize the magnitude and distribution of spatial T1 variation and provide a quantitative framework for assessing intralesional heterogeneity. This review summarizes the biological rationale, technical principles, and emerging evidence regarding Gd-EOB-DTPA-enhanced T1 mapping for the assessment of intranodular heterogeneity. It further discusses its potential role in malignant transformation risk stratification of cirrhotic nodules, current limitations, and future directions for clinical translation.

articles.title: Pipeline Dependence of Structural Brain MRI Morphometry: A Systematic Review of Agreement Across Software, Versions, and Processing Choices.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Morphometric measurements from structural brain MRI are sensitive to analysis pipelines and software versions. PURPOSE: To evaluate inter-pipeline agreement, reliability, and systematic measurement differences across automated morphometric software packages on identical structural MRI datasets. STUDY TYPE: Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD420261456493). POPULATION: One hundred eleven studies comprising healthy and clinical cohorts across the lifespan. FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: Predominantly 1.5 T and 3 T, with 7 T data also included. ASSESSMENT: Automated and semi-automated processing pipelines (predominantly FreeSurfer, FSL, and SPM/CAT) evaluated for brain volumes and cortical thickness. STATISTICAL TESTS: Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), Pearson/Spearman correlation (r), Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC), and Bland-Altman bias (p < 0.05). RESULTS: Agreement varied across anatomical regions, software pairs, versions, and processing conditions. Strong associations coexisted with systematic measurement differences in several comparisons, but neither high association nor high agreement was consistent across global and regional outputs. Manual-reference comparisons showed structure- and population-dependent volume overestimation, with rankings differing by outcome metric. Cortical thickness, intracranial-volume normalization, and normative percentiles showed additional method-dependent differences. Software updates and preprocessing choices altered measurements and, in some studies, downstream findings. Computational repeatability, anatomical accuracy, and longitudinal-change agreement represented distinct properties and did not consistently favor the same method. DATA CONCLUSION: High correlation or consistency does not ensure absolute agreement or interchangeability in MRI morphometry. Regional discrepancies vary across software pairs, versions, and processing conditions, limiting generalization of individual comparisons to other methods or populations. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 1. TECHNICAL EFFICACY STAGE: Stage 2.

articles.title: A Comprehensive Radiomics Model for Predicting Progression-Free Survival in High-Risk Neuroblastoma Based on CT Imaging.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This study evaluates the predictive utility of clinical features, CT imaging characteristics, radiomic features, and multimodal statistical models in estimating progression-free survival (PFS) in high-risk neuroblastoma (NB) patients. MATERIALS AND METHODS: 105 pathologically confirmed high - risk NB patients per COG criteria were retrospectively selected and divided into training (80%) and test sets (20%). Statistical models were built using clinical variables, CT features, and radiomic features, with SVM algorithms employed. Five models were assessed, including radiomics, clinical + CT, clinical + radiomics, imaging + radiomics, and combined clinical + CT + radiomics models. A nomogram was constructed to predict PFS. RESULTS: Univariate analysis found NSE > 200 μg/mL, LDH >1000 U/L, and MYCN amplification as significant poor - prognosis predictors (P < 0.05). Multivariate analysis confirmed MYCN amplification (P = 0.043) and IDRFs presence (P = 0.036) as independent risk factors. A radiomics model was built from CT scans' different phases. The combined model showed the best and most stable performance with AUC values of 0.855, 0.796, 0.856 in training, validation, and test cohorts. A nomogram integrating Rad - Score and clinical parameters from Cox regression was developed, with a C - index of 0.806 (P = 0.028) via bootstrap validation. CONCLUSION: This study validates a PFS predictive model combining clinical, CT, and radiomic features, providing a robust tool for individualized prognosis in high-risk NB patients. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: Radiomics demonstrates predictive utility for progression-free survival in pediatric patients with high-risk neuroblastoma.

articles.title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Procedural Efficiency of ACR TI-RADS, EU-TIRADS, and K-TIRADS in ≤ 10 mm Thyroid Nodules Using Bethesda Cytology: A Cohort of 998 Nodules.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare the diagnostic performance and procedural efficiency of American College of Radiology Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (ACR TI-RADS), European Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (EU-TIRADS), and Korean Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (K-TIRADS) in ≤ 10 mm nodules using Bethesda cytology as the reference standard. METHODS: This retrospective study included 998 nodules ≤10 mm undergoing ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB). Primary analyses included Bethesda II (negative) and Bethesda V-VI (positive) nodules excluding Bethesda I/III/IV, yielding 604 nodules (540 negative; 64 positive). Categories 1-3 were considered low risk and 4-5 high risk under a harmonized threshold Diagnostic performance and classification patterns were compared. RESULTS: K-TIRADS showed the numerically highest sensitivity (93.8%) and negative predictive value (NPV) (97.9%), although sensitivity did not differ significantly between systems, with lower specificity (35.4%) and accuracy (41.6%).EU-TIRADS showed intermediate performans (sensitivity 68.8%, specificity 73.7%, accuracy 73.2%). ACR TI-RADS achieved the highest specificity (83.3%) and accuracy (81.0%) with lower sensitivity (60.9%). Low-risk classification rates were 78.6% (ACR), 69.2% (EU), and 32.3% (K) of nodules; false-positive high-risk classifications among Bethesda II nodules were 16.7%, 26.3%, and 64.6%, respectively. CONCLUSION: In ≤ 10 mm nodules, the three systems demonstrated distinct diagnostic and classification profiles under a harmonized TR4-5 threshold, with different trade-offs between sensitivity and specificity. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: Applying a harmonized TR4-5 threshold in ≤ 10 mm nodules reveals substantially differences in classification patterns among the three systems, demonstrating that they are not interchangeable under a uniform risk threshold.

articles.title: Diffusion posterior sampling framework for joint image reconstruction and scatter estimation in cone-beam CT.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: X-ray scatter can have a significant impact on image quality in cone beam CT (CBCT) including the introduction of severe artifacts and CT value inaccuracies. Classic solutions to the scatter problem often involve specialized hardware and data acquisition, or computationally expensive estimation of scatter via Monte Carlo (MC) methods. PURPOSE: We explore a novel scatter correction approach that leverages the recent development of Diffusion Posterior Sampling (DPS) to jointly estimate CT attenuation and scattered radiation directly from single-energy CT projection data. METHODS: We rewrite the nonlinear forward model for CT measurements to include an unknown additive scatter term which we jointly estimate with the image volume. Solution of this ill-posed problem is enabled by diffusion models that capture the distribution of scatter-free images of anatomy. The joint reconstruction and scatter estimation is evaluated using both simulation and phantom data and compared with a MC-based scatter correction method. RESULTS: Qualitative and quantitative results obtained from simulated and phantom data shows that the proposed approach can effectively estimate the scatter contribution, significantly remove scatter artifacts, and restore the overall image contrast and attenuation values. CONCLUSIONS: Joint estimation of scatter and reconstruction for CBCT has the potential to provide improved CBCT image quality and quantitation through direct estimation without the addition of specialized hardware or MC simulations.

articles.title: Rapid coronary computed tomography angiography-derived fractional flow reserve: A feasibility study for on-site assessment.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Fractional flow reserve (FFR) is the reference standard for physiological assessment of coronary artery stenosis severity, but invasive measurement requires catheterization and hyperemic agents. Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA)-derived FFR offers a non-invasive alternative, though existing approaches based on computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are computationally intensive and impractical for on-site clinical use. PURPOSE: To evaluate the feasibility of rapidly estimating FFR from CCTA using three mathematical, centerline-based computational methodologies. This study investigates whether pressure-drop formulations relying solely on coronary geometric information can provide rapid FFR estimates suitable for potential on-site clinical application, without the need for computationally intensive fluid dynamics simulations. METHODS: Three CCTA-derived FFR methodologies were evaluated: fixed Fractional Flow Reserve (fFFR3D), mathematical virtual Functional Assessment Index (mvFAI3D), and tomographic Fractional Flow Reserve (tomoFFR). Each method uses the patient mean arterial pressure (MAP) along with the coronary centerline geometry to characterize vessel dimensions and estimate pressure loss under hyperemic conditions. fFFR3D assumes a fixed hyperaemic blood velocity of 0.35 m/s; mvFAI3D extends the virtual Functional Assessment Index (vFAI) using a mathematical pressure-drop formulation; and tomoFFR estimates hyperaemic flow and pressure loss using a baseline fixed-velocity approach. Fourteen coronary vessels from a publicly available dataset with reference invasive FFR measurements were analyzed. Predicted FFR values were compared with clinical measurements (wire measured FFR), with emphasis on classification relative to the clinical threshold of FFR = 0.80  and on computational time. RESULTS: Relative to the FFR = 0.80 threshold, fFFR3D and tomoFFR correctly classified 12 of the 14 vessels (85.7%) and mvFAI3D correctly classified 11 of the 14 vessels (78.6%). Given the limited sample size, no definitive conclusions regarding diagnostic accuracy or generalizability can be drawn. Nevertheless, the results demonstrate the feasibility of applying mathematical pressure-drop models directly to CCTA-derived coronary centerlines. Once centerlines were available, all three approaches required less than 1 s to calculate FFR, enabling substantially faster estimation than conventional CFD-based approaches and supporting potential integration into on-site CCTA analysis workflows. CONCLUSIONS: These findings demonstrate the feasibility of rapid, centerline-based CCTA-derived FFR estimation using mathematical models of coronary pressure loss. Sub-second computational time, combined with the availability of automated AI-based coronary centerline extraction and physician correction in contemporary CCTA workstations, provides a potential pathway toward on-site FFR assessment during routine CT interpretation. Larger prospective, multicenter studies with invasive FFR reference measurements are required to establish diagnostic accuracy, reproducibility, and clinical robustness prior to clinical implementation.

articles.title: Evaluation Design and Model Selection Stability in Medical Image Classification Benchmarks: A Multi-dataset Study.
articles.abstract: Medical image classification benchmarks inform model selection. We assessed how data splits, training seeds, and evaluation conditions affect selection stability and whether repeated evaluation budgets support reproducible rankings. The original study comprised 800 runs on OrganAMNIST and SIPaKMeD, using four ImageNet-initialized convolutional neural networks (CNNs), ten splits, five seeds, and two checkpoint selection and stopping procedures. The 300-run extension evaluated the International Skin Imaging Collaboration (ISIC) 2019 challenge dataset and MURA (musculoskeletal radiographs) using four CNNs, ten splits, and three seeds under procedure A; paired Swin Transformer-Tiny (Swin-T) analyses used five splits and three seeds. Balanced accuracy (BA) defined rankings. Paired resampling quantified selection frequencies and uncertainty; budget analyses compared discovery subsets with held-out splits. Single-context agreement with the full repeated evaluation reference was 44-62% in original strata, 90% for ISIC 2019, and 60% for MURA. The two procedures changed selected identities in 46% of OrganAMNIST and 56% of SIPaKMeD contexts. On matched five-split, three-seed contexts with shared preprocessing, adding Swin-T changed leave-one-split-out agreement from 86.7 to 20.0% in ISIC 2019 and from 66.7 to 80.0% in MURA. At five discovery splits and three seeds, agreement with held-out references ranged from 20.4 to 89.0% in original strata, reaching 100% for ISIC 2019 and 57.1% for MURA. Agreement did not increase uniformly across evaluated budgets. Repeated evaluation revealed both stable and changing selections. Reporting performance alongside selection stability informs budgeting and whether to advance one candidate or retain a shortlist.

articles.title: An Interpretable Multimodal Deep Learning Framework Integrating MRI and Clinical Data via Bidirectional Cross-Modal Attention for Improved Cardiac Disease Detection.
articles.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases continue to be the primary cause of mortality worldwide; however, precise diagnosis is often limited by dependence on individual data modalities and the unclear nature of traditional deep learning models. In this study, we introduce an explainable multimodal deep learning framework that simultaneously analyzes cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and structured clinical variables through a bidirectional cross-modal attention mechanism that operates on token sequences. The architecture utilizes modality-specific encoders ResNet-50 for imaging and a multilayer perceptron for clinical data interconnected through attention that dynamically aligns complementary information, reducing feature dilution and modal dominance. A multitask objective that includes classification, contrastive alignment (InfoNCE), and regularization further reinforces semantic consistency across modalities. Integrated post hoc explainability modules, such as Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping for spatial localization and SHapley Additive exPlanations for clinical feature attribution, offer transparent decision support. Tested on a cohort of 12,847 patients using fivefold cross-validation, the framework achieved an accuracy of 94.2% and an area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve of 0.97, significantly surpassing unimodal and traditional multimodal baselines (p < 0.01). The explanations generated showed 91% concordance with independent cardiologist evaluations. The findings presented herein were derived through internal five-fold cross-validation conducted at a solitary tertiary care institution, thereby substantiating internal validity while limiting multicenter generalizability; consequently, external validation is requisite for broader applicability. These results demonstrate that attention-driven multimodal fusion, combined with post hoc explainability, provides both strong diagnostic performance and clinically useful transparency, positioning the framework as a promising internally validated approach and a foundation for future external validation.

articles.title: Advanced diffusion models in real-world glioma assessment: A comparative analysis of diagnostic performance, pathological correlations, and prognostic value.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Various advanced diffusion models have shown robust diagnostic performance in glioma assessment, yet their relative efficacy has not been comprehensively evaluated. This study aimed to compare continuous-time random walk (CTRW), free water corrected-diffusion tensor imaging (FW-DTI), and mean apparent propagator (MAP) in predicting isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) status and Ki-67 levels of gliomas, investigate their associations with tumor microenvironment (TME) markers, and evaluate their prognostic value in IDH-wildtype patients. METHODS: This retrospective study included 151 patients (83 men; mean age, 47.45 years) with gliomas. CTRW, FW-DTI, MAP, and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) were processed from diffusion spectrum imaging (DSI), and mean parameter values were extracted. Logistic regression assessed model performance for predicting IDH status and Ki-67 levels. Correlation and Cox regression analyses evaluated their associations with TME markers and prognosis, respectively. RESULTS: CTRW, FW-DTI, MAP, and the combined models showed higher diagnostic performance than ADC, with the combined models achieved the highest numerical AUCs (AUCs 0.930 and 0.859) in identifying IDH status and Ki-67 levels. Except for ADC, no statistically significant differences were observed in diagnostic performance among these models. Additionally, multiple advanced diffusion parameters showed correlations with TME markers, and MAP showed associations with overall survival for IDH-wildtype patients (HR = 4.070, P = 0.020). CONCLUSION: CTRW, FW-DTI, and MAP showed similar predictive performance and outperformed ADC for IDH status and tumor proliferation in gliomas. Their associations with TME markers and the prognostic relevance of MAP support the potential of advanced diffusion imaging for noninvasive pathological and prognostic assessment of gliomas.

articles.title: MRI-derived synthetic [¹⁸F]FET PET in neuro-oncology: evaluation in glioma grading and differentiation from solitary brain metastasis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: O-(2-[18F]fluoroethyl)-L-tyrosine positron emission tomography ([18F]FET PET) is clinically useful in neuro-oncology but limited by cost and availability. We assessed the clinical utility of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived synthetic [18F]FET PET. METHODS: A total of 489 patients with histologically confirmed gliomas or brain metastases were retrospectively analyzed. A deep learning model generated synthetic PET images from multimodal MRI in the overall cohort and subgroups. Synthetic PET was evaluated against reference PET for image similarity by peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM), standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR) analysis by Pearson correlation and Bland-Altman analysis, and blinded reader assessment for glioma grading and high-grade glioma (HGG) versus solitary brain metastasis (SBM) differentiation using receiver operating characteristic analysis with area under the curve (AUC). RESULTS: Synthetic PET showed high similarity to reference PET in the overall, glioma, and metastasis groups (PSNR, 34.7-35.5 dB; SSIM, 0.90-0.96), and SUVR correlations were strong (r = 0.77-0.93, all P < 0.001), with minimal bias and narrow limits of agreement. Compared with MRI alone, MRI with synthetic PET improved glioma grading and HGG-SBM differentiation, increasing AUC from 0.815 to 0.941 and from 0.816 to 0.901 for glioma grading and from 0.731 to 0.871 and from 0.784 to 0.872 for HGG-SBM differentiation across the 2 readers (all P < 0.05). No significant differences were found between MRI with synthetic and reference PET for either task (all P > 0.05). CONCLUSIONS: MRI-derived synthetic [18F]FET PET may enhance glioma grading and HGG-SBM differentiation, providing a PET-like alternative when FET PET is unavailable.

articles.title: Quantitative evaluation of cervical foraminal stenosis and nerve root diameter using MRI-based multiplanar reconstruction: a prospective study.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Accurate evaluation of cervical foraminal stenosis using conventional MRI is challenging. We quantitatively evaluated cervical foraminal and nerve root diameters using MRI-based multiplanar reconstruction (MPR) and compared measurements between the proximal-type cervical spondylotic amyotrophy (CSA) and cervical spondylotic radiculopathy (CSR) groups. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Twenty-eight consecutive patients were prospectively enrolled: 16 with CSA and C4/5 foraminal stenosis; 12 with CSR without symptomatic C4/5 involvement. T2-weighted coronal MRI was obtained, and images perpendicular to the C4/5 foramen were reconstructed. Foraminal height and anteroposterior diameter, as well as the craniocaudal and anteroposterior diameters of the C5 nerve root, were measured. Side-to-side comparisons were performed in CSA, and measurements were also compared with those in CSR. RESULTS: In CSA, foraminal height was significantly smaller on the symptomatic side than on the asymptomatic side (p = 0.042). The anteroposterior diameters of the C4/5 foramen and C5 nerve root were significantly smaller on the symptomatic side (2.4 ± 0.4 mm vs. 3.1 ± 0.5 mm and 1.9 ± 0.4 mm vs. 2.7 ± 0.5 mm, respectively, p < 0.001). Compared with CSR, the symptomatic side in CSA showed significantly smaller anteroposterior diameters of both the foramen and the nerve root, whereas no significant differences were observed between the asymptomatic side in CSA and CSR. CONCLUSION: MRI-based MPR allows quantitative evaluation of cervical foraminal narrowing and nerve root diameter. Focal anteroposterior narrowing of the C4/5 foramen with reduced diameter of the C5 nerve root was associated with the symptomatic side in CSA.

articles.title: Explainable radiomics and clinical models for prediction of total knee arthroplasty in knee osteoarthritis: data from Osteoarthritis Initiative.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To develop and evaluate MRI radiomics models, with and without clinical variables, for predicting total knee arthroplasty (TKA) within 9 years in patients with knee osteoarthritis. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective exploratory study included 507 participants from the Osteoarthritis Initiative-Zuse Institute Berlin dataset with manually segmented knee MRIs; 66 underwent TKA. Four hundred radiomics features from bone and cartilage were combined with 13 clinical variables. Logistic regression, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression, and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) were evaluated using radiomics-only, clinical-only, and combined feature sets in an 80/20 development-holdout analysis and stratified nested cross-validation. Preprocessing, feature selection, and tuning were restricted to training folds. RESULTS: On the held-out test set, radiomics-only LASSO had the highest observed AUC-ROC of 0.76 (95% CI, 0.61-0.88), followed closely by combined LASSO at 0.75 (0.61-0.87). Combined logistic regression and XGBoost achieved AUC-ROC values of 0.73 (0.60-0.86) and 0.72 (0.57-0.84), respectively. Differences among the leading models were modest. In nested cross-validation, combined LASSO showed the highest discrimination (AUC-ROC, 0.786 [0.722-0.841]; AUC-PR, 0.343 [0.239-0.451]; F1 score, 0.405 [0.321-0.481]), with modest improvement over radiomics-only LASSO (AUC-ROC, 0.781 [0.717-0.834]). Consistently retained predictors included femoral bone sphericity, femoral cartilage first-order skewness, and WOMAC disability. CONCLUSION: MRI radiomics features, alone or combined with clinical variables, showed potential for predicting TKA risk. Performance differences among leading models were modest, and these exploratory findings require external validation before clinical application.

articles.title: Simulation-Based Multidisciplinary Training for Contrast Reaction Management: Learner-Reported Preparedness and Teamwork Outcomes.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Acute contrast reactions are rare but potentially life-threatening events that require rapid recognition, technical proficiency, and coordinated multidisciplinary team responses. Simulation-based education may address gaps in preparedness for these high-acuity, low-frequency emergencies in radiology departments. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A retrospective educational study of a high-fidelity contrast reaction simulation implemented at a single academic medical center was performed. Participants included radiologists, radiology trainees, technologists, and nursing staff. Following the session, participants completed an anonymous survey assessing realism, clinical applicability, perceived impact on teamwork, technical skills, clinical judgment, and anticipated effects on patient safety using a 5-point Likert scale. Free-text responses were analyzed using thematic analysis. RESULTS: Ninety-eight participants completed the survey. Across all evaluated domains, more than 90% of respondents rated the simulation as Very Good or Excellent. Participants reported perceived improvements in teamwork and communication, technical and procedural skills, recognition and management of adverse contrast reactions, and application of institutional treatment algorithms. Qualitative analysis identified recurrent themes of improved closed-loop communication, earlier escalation of care, increased familiarity with emergency equipment, and greater self-reported confidence in managing contrast reactions. CONCLUSION: A multidisciplinary, simulation-based contrast reaction management program was associated with high learner engagement and perceived improvements in preparedness, teamwork, and patient safety, as per self-reported outcomes. Simulation training represents a feasible and effective strategy for preparing radiology teams to manage high-acuity, low-frequency contrast emergencies.

articles.title: Device Education in Interventional Radiology: Development of a Structured Visual Atlas.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Interventional radiology (IR) learners must connect device appearance and label information with function, compatibility, and procedural role, while distinguishing related devices. We developed The IR Table Book, a structured visual atlas, to provide a consistent framework for foundational device education. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The first author developed the atlas in 2026 for learners beginning supervised IR training. Devices were organized by family, function, procedure, and workflow role. Each entry used three panels: Visual Recognition, Use & Procedural Context, and Key Distinctions. Separate orientation sections addressed label interpretation and workflows. An IR resident coauthor reviewed all 171 entries for clinical and factual accuracy; a second physician coauthor reviewed the framework and manuscript. Technical quality assurance checked tracking codes, device names, section assignments, and recorded page locations against the assembled atlas. RESULTS: The First Edition 2027 atlas comprised 171 entries across 18 sections. Technical checks confirmed assembly completeness and recorded page locations in the 104-page atlas, with no unresolved rendering defects. A physician coauthor reviewed clinical and factual accuracy; formal independent content validation and learner evaluation are planned but have not yet been conducted. CONCLUSION: The atlas provides a framework for IR device education. Independent content validation and learner evaluation remain necessary.

articles.title: Development and Evaluation of MagnetXplorers: An Interactive Mystery Game for Medical Imaging Education.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Escape games have emerged as engaging educational tools in medical education but have primarily targeted advanced medical students and healthcare professionals. Here, we present MagnetXplorers, an interactive mystery game designed to introduce upper-secondary school students to medical imaging, radiology, and the interdisciplinary foundations of modern healthcare technologies. MATERIALS AND METHODS: MagnetXplorers was developed using a design-based research approach and implemented as an outreach workshop at a university hospital. Participants completed hands-on activities covering ultrasound, X-ray, computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which collectively contributed to solving a fictional diagnostic case. Accompanying teachers participated in guided interviews analyzed using qualitative content analysis. RESULTS: Nine workshops have been successfully conducted. The final workshop concept and all accompanying materials were released as open educational resources, including construction manuals and MRI-scanner-independent alternatives. Teachers evaluated the workshop positively, highlighting its authentic clinical context, interdisciplinary integration of medicine, physics, and engineering, as well as the combination of experiments, simulations, image analysis, and gamified problem-solving. CONCLUSION: MagnetXplorers provides an accessible, transferable educational concept for introducing learners to medical imaging using low-cost experimental setups. The positive evaluation supports the potential of gamified interdisciplinary learning to promote interest in radiology and science, technology, engineering, and mathematics disciplines.

articles.title: Video-based Deep Learning for Pulmonary Embolism Classification on Paired Contrast-enhanced and Noncontrast Chest CT: A Single-center Retrospective Feasibility Study.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a disease that is difficult to diagnose because its clinical findings are nonspecific and it carries high mortality when not treated early. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA), the gold standard for diagnosis, cannot be performed in every patient because of contraindications related to contrast medium; Noncontrast computed tomography (NCCT), on the other hand, cannot be used as a reliable tool for exclusion because of its low sensitivity. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective study, the paired images of 716 patients (129 PE-positive, 587 PE-negative) who had undergone both CTPA and NCCT on the same day between 2018 and 2026 were examined. The availability of two scans obtained from the same patient on the same day provided a paired cohort in which clinical and anatomical variables other than the presence of contrast were largely held constant, so that the CTPA scan established with certainty where a thrombus lay in each patient whose noncontrast scan was analyzed. Each scan was converted into a 12-second mediastinal-window video, from which a 40-frame segment centered on the temporal midpoint of the recording was extracted for analysis. For the automatic detection of thrombus, three-dimensional deep learning architectures have been developed: PureStream-3D, BiLSTM-ResNet-3D based on bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM), and AttnFocus-3D based on an attention mechanism. The models have been optimized with different training configurations to address class imbalance, and the dataset has been divided at the patient level into 70% training, 20% validation, and 10% independent test sets. RESULTS: In the CTPA test set, the highest discrimination has been achieved by the AttnFocus-3D-1 model (accuracy 0.9306; area under the curve [AUC] 0.98), whereas the most balanced sensitivity-specificity profile has been obtained with the BiLSTM-ResNet-3D-2 variant (sensitivity 0.9138, specificity 0.8571). In the NCCT test set, the AttnFocus-3D-2 architecture has reached an accuracy of 0.9306, an AUC of 0.97, a sensitivity of 0.9655, and a specificity of 0.7857. CONCLUSION: Taken together, these findings indicate that the developed deep learning approaches are strong in confirming the presence or absence of PE and can be considered as a decision-support infrastructure in clinical scenarios with high diagnostic uncertainty.

articles.title: Transcatheter Arterial Embolization for Pediatric Renal Trauma: A National Trauma Data Bank Analysis (2017-2024).
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To describe pediatric renal embolization outcomes and compare transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE) with surgery and conservative management in transfused children with high-grade renal trauma. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Children younger than 18 years undergoing kidney embolization in the National Trauma Data Bank (2017-2024; n=101) were assessed using registry-based clinical-success proxies. Transfused American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) grade III-V patients were classified as TAE (n=86), therapeutic renal surgery (n=348), or conservative management (n=634). Separate propensity models supported 1:1 matching without replacement for TAE versus surgery and conservative management, exactly by grade, age band, and blunt/penetrating mechanism. Mortality included emergency department and inpatient deaths. RESULTS: Median time to embolization was 3.08 hours. Primary and secondary clinical success were 90/101 (89.1%) and 93/101 (92.1%). Under the broader composite, primary success was lower after penetrating than blunt injury (68.8% vs 92.7%; P=.016), but the renal-specific comparison was inconclusive (P=.253). TAE was used in 5.7% of transfused grade III-V injuries. In 59 TAE-surgery pairs, mortality was 6/59 (10.2%) versus 10/59 (16.9%; conditional odds ratio [cOR] 0.56, 95% CI 0.15-1.85; P=.424). In 70 TAE-conservative pairs, mortality was 7/70 (10.0%) in each arm (cOR 1.00, 95% CI 0.27-3.74; P=1.000). Measured injury and admission-year imbalance remained. CONCLUSIONS: Nearly 9 of 10 children avoided qualifying reintervention after kidney embolization. The penetrating-injury association included potentially extra-renal laparotomy and did not establish greater renal-specific embolization failure. Matched mortality comparisons were inconclusive.

articles.title: Toxicity and patient-reported quality of life through 12 months following pelvis-inclusive once-weekly stereotactic body radiotherapy versus conventional IMRT for high-risk prostate cancer: updated results of the SRAM randomized phase II trial.
articles.abstract: AIM: To compare toxicity through 12 months and patient-reported quality of life following pelvis-inclusive stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) versus conventional intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) in men with high-risk prostate cancer enrolled in the SRAM trial (NCT03938649). METHODS: Men with node-negative high-risk prostate cancer were randomly assigned 1:1 to pelvis-inclusive SBRT or IMRT. SBRT was delivered 40 Gy to the prostate and 25 Gy to the pelvis in five once-weekly fractions; IMRT comprised 50 Gy to the prostate and pelvis followed by a 26 Gy prostate boost. Gastrointestinal (GI) and genitourinary (GU) toxicities were graded using Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 4.0. Patient-reported outcomes were assessed using the Expanded Prostate Cancer Index (EPIC) and International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS). RESULTS: Among 121 evaluable patients, 60 received SBRT and 61 IMRT. Between 6 and 12 months after radiotherapy, grade ≥2 GI and GU toxicity occurred in 16.7 % versus 13.1 % (p = 0.583) and 11.7 % versus 16.4 % (p = 0.455) of patients, respectively, including one grade 3 rectal hemorrhage after SBRT. EPIC bowel scores were lower in the SBRT group at 9 months (83.2 vs. 92.4; p = 0.0022) and 12 months (82.5 vs. 90.1; p = 0.0181), reflecting greater declines from baseline. Other EPIC domains and IPSS outcomes were broadly similar between groups. CONCLUSION: Once-weekly pelvis-inclusive SBRT showed no significant difference in grade ≥2 GI and GU toxicity compared with conventional IMRT at 6-12 months, but was associated with worse patient-reported bowel quality of life at 9-12 months.

articles.title: Transcranial photobiomodulation influences BOLD responses during finger sequence execution: An fMRI Study in young and older adults.
articles.abstract: Transcranial photobiomodulation (PBM) is an emerging non-invasive brain stimulation method that is thought to increase neural metabolism by stimulating ATP production by the mitochondria. However, the mechanisms of action and the effects on the human brain are still unclear. In the present study, we investigated the potential of this method to enhance Blood Oxygen Level Dependent (BOLD) responses during the execution of a motor task in young and aged participants. Sixty young and aged participants were included in this single-blinded, sham-controlled, randomised, crossover study. They underwent an fMRI recording before and after 24-min stimulation with an 80-LED helmet emitting transcranially red and near infrared light. Post vs Pre BOLD signal was compared between PBM and SHAM, in each group. At baseline, aged participants showed reduced BOLD signal compared to young ones, in key regions of sensorimotor processing, principally the left primary motor cortex and striatum. Transcranial PBM did not have a real impact in the young group. In aged participants, analysis performed on the whole brain did not reveal widespread changes, but rather local increases in BOLD responses in the right ventral premotor cortex and insula. More specifically, a regional analysis further showed increased BOLD responses in the left primary motor cortex, and right dorsal and ventral premotor regions and striatum. Some of these regions were under-activated at baseline in aged participants relative to the young ones. These results suggest that transcranial PBM can increase fMRI BOLD responses locally in some task-related regions in aged subjects. Further research is needed to distinguish neural from vascular effects in transcranial PBM.

articles.title: Deep learning-based estimation of multi-tracer PET phenotypes from structural MRI for A/T/N-related analysis and progression prediction in Alzheimer's disease.
articles.abstract: Early identification and staging of Alzheimer's disease (AD) require integrated assessment of amyloid deposition, tau pathology, and neurodegeneration. PET provides spatially resolved in vivo imaging biomarkers, but its routine use is constrained by cost, tracer availability, and radiation exposure, limiting access to complete A/T/N imaging profiles. We propose a conditional flow matching-based framework that estimates SUV-space PET-derived phenotypes related to 18F-FDG, 18F-florbetapir and 18F-flortaucipir from a single T1-weighted MRI scan. To address limitations in SUV-level quantitative fidelity, single-tracer applicability, and external generalization, the framework combines a PET prior network with a time-conditioned velocity network and uses multi-constraint losses to preserve SUV accuracy, regional uptake consistency, and anatomical boundaries. The model was developed using 1,978 paired ADNI MRI-PET records from 991 participants and evaluated in a predefined ADNI test set and an independent hospital PET/MR cohort of 514 participants. In ADNI, voxel-level MAEs were 0.012, 0.034, and 0.021 SUV, with representative ROI Pearson correlations of 0.978, 0.842, and 0.781. In the hospital cohort, corresponding MAEs were 0.014, 0.037, and 0.024 SUV, with ROI correlations of 0.952, 0.803, and 0.834. In OASIS, generated PET-derived features improved CDR stratification and future cognitive decline prediction, increasing AUCs from 0.662 to 0.739 and from 0.569 to 0.643. These findings suggest that the method can provide PET-derived phenotypes related to A/T/N analysis from structural MRI when PET is unavailable, but should not be interpreted as a replacement for molecular PET assessment.

articles.title: The anatomo-functional organization of the indirect pallido-subthalamic pathway in humans combining histology and diffusion imaging.
articles.abstract: The subthalamic nucleus (STN) integrates cortical motor and emotional information with a posterior motor domain and an anterior limbic domain. However, the detailed anatomo-functional organisation of the STN in humans remains incomplete, largely because the indirect pathway linking the STN and the external globus pallidus (GPe) is difficult to image. Here, we characterize the GPe-STN pathway using histology combined with high-resolution diffusion imaging. We scanned three ex vivo specimens at 11.7 Tesla and ten healthy volunteers at 3 Tesla with ultra-high gradient. Brain sections were immunostained, reconstructed in 3D, and registered to define regions of interest in both datasets. Structural connectivity was assessed using probabilistic tractography (MRtrix), with homogeneously distributed seed points to maximize streamlines reconstruction. We found that GPe-STN streamlines follow fiber bundles that traverse or bypass the internal GP and the internal capsule, ex and in vivo. Ex vivo tractography revealed distinct projection patterns of limbic, associative, and sensorimotor GPe streamlines, targeting the anteromedial STN (24% volume coverage) and the posterocentral STN (67% and 30% coverage, respectively). In vivo tractography revealed a similar spatial organization, particularly in the right hemisphere, with consistent patterns across individuals. A substantial overlap was observed between associative and sensorimotor territories, whereas the limbic territory appeared more segregated. The data-driven clustering of the STN based on GPe-connectivity fingerprints confirms these findings. These results challenge the classical tripartite model of the basal ganglia and provide new insights into the STN anatomo-functional organization and support individualized targeting for functional neurosurgery.

articles.title: Closed-form, engine-portable uncertainty prediction of deformable image registration for dose accumulation in adaptive radiotherapy.
articles.abstract: Voxel-level uncertainty estimates of the deformation vector field (DVF) produced by commercial deformable image registration (DIR) engines are flagged as an open issue by AAPM TG-132 but seldom available, preventing principled propagation into accumulated dose-volume histograms (DVHs). We propose and validate an engine-portable per-voxel σ predictor for the DVF (μ) of a deterministic DIR, calibrated by one scalar f against landmark Target Registration Error (TRE), with no access to the engine's internals.Approach. The framework combines (i) an anisotropic Gaussian correlation kernel, longer along the cranio-caudal axis, generalising the isotropic kernel of Smolders et al. (2023); and (ii) a heuristic-residual σ_h=f[wR̃+(1-w)d̃] (default w=0.7), where R̃ combines a self-similarity descriptor residual with an image-gradient suppression factor and d̃ is |Jacobian determinant-1|, both normalised to [0,1]; σ_h is closed-form, computed from the image pair and the DVF without optimisation or training. For each combination of dataset and DIR engine (a cell), f is calibrated against TRE via grid search minimising the Landmark Expected Calibration Error (LECE).Main results. Across 4 publicly annotated computed tomography datasets (Lung-, Abdominal- and Liver-DIR-QA and DIR-LAB Castillo; 44,778 landmarks) and 4 DIR engines (ANTs SyNRA, ConvexAdam, uniGradICON, Elastix), with f fitted on other patients (5-fold cross-validation), the calibrated σ_h achieves, in the per-direction convention of Smolders et al., LECE within or below their 0.41-1.34mm range in all 16 cells (cases with final root-mean-square TRE ≤10mm retained). A constant σ calibrated likewise also meets this range, but the variation of σ_h raises the held-out log-likelihood in 13 cells; σ_h ranks landmarks by error only weakly (Spearman ρ=-0.11 to +0.34).Significance. A one-scalar, post-hoc calibration yields voxel-level DVF uncertainty for any deterministic DIR that exports its DVF, partly addressing the AAPM TG-132 gap; propagation into accumulated DVH bands is illustrated on one lung stereotactic body radiotherapy case.

articles.title: Mesh-based detailed human kidney models of the ICRP reference adults for radiopharmaceutical therapy dosimetry: microscale model of the renal cortex.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) is a rapidly evolving field in oncology, driven by advances in molecular targeting, such as prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA), and the use of radionuclides with different radiation emissions, including beta emitters and alpha emitters. RPT is typically used to treat disseminated cancers, where dosimetry-based treatment planning aims to limit radiation exposure to normal organs and reduce toxicity. This study aimed to develop a three-dimensional, histology-informed model of the human renal cortical labyrinth to support microscale dosimetry and the development of dose-response models for renal toxicity in RPT. The microscale model was dosimetrically coupled to an improved macroscale kidney model within the ICRP reference adult male and female phantoms. APPROACH: Histological human kidney sections were serially imaged using a high-resolution digital camera mounted on a light microscope. The images were imported into 3D Slicer for volumetric reconstruction. Renal corpuscles were manually segmented, and convoluted tubules were mapped using centerline luminal markers. Glomeruli were reconstructed by stitching segmented slices and scaling them to match diameters measured in 3D Slicer. Bowman's capsules were modeled to surround each glomerulus. Proximal and distal convoluted tubules (PCTs and DCTs) were created using a multi-pipe function. MAIN RESULTS: The final microscale model included seven renal corpuscles with their respective PCTs and DCTs, embedded within a representative microenvironment containing tubule fragments, blood vessels, and extracellular tissue. Absorbed fractions were calculated for multiple source-target combinations. These microscale dosimetry results were coupled with corresponding macroscale kidney dosimetry to generate S-values for more than 1200 radionuclides. SIGNIFICANCE: A three-dimensional, histology-informed model of the human renal cortical labyrinth was developed from H&E-stained kidney sections to represent the principal components of the nephron and its surrounding microenvironment. Coupling the microscale and macroscale models provides a framework for evaluating radionuclide-specific energy deposition at both spatial scales.

articles.title: Mesh-based detailed human kidney models of the ICRP reference adults for radiopharmaceutical therapy dosimetry: macroscale models.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: In radiopharmaceutical therapy, the kidney is a major dose-limiting organ for many radiopharmaceuticals. The ICRP adult mesh-type reference computational phantoms (MRCPs) define the kidneys only with cortex, medulla, and pelvis regions, limiting the ability to characterize heterogeneous dose distributions within the kidneys. The present study aims to develop anatomically detailed macroscale kidney models for the adult MRCPs-comprising the capsule, cortex, medullary pyramids, papillae, pelvis wall, pelvis epithelium, and urine. APPROACH: The cortex, medullary pyramids, and papillae were constructed by segmenting 15 cadaveric kidney specimens and scaling them in accordance with the reference volumes and location, whereas the capsule, pelvis wall, pelvis epithelium, and urine were constructed based on target thicknesses. The developed models were integrated into the MRCPs and implemented in PHITS Monte Carlo code to compute absorbed fractions and specific absorbed fractions (SAFs) for photons, electrons, and alpha particles. The S values for clinically relevant therapeutic and diagnostic radionuclides were then derived using the SAF dataset and the ICRP Publication 107 decay data. MAIN RESULTS: Anatomically detailed macroscale kidney models were developed for the adult male and female in a tetrahedral mesh format. The total masses were matched to the ICRP reference masses within 0.1% deviation. Compared with the original MRCP kidneys, the new kidney models produced substantial differences in SAFs, particularly for source-target combinations involving the renal pelvis, reflecting the more anatomically detailed representation of the collecting system. These differences resulted in corresponding differences in S values, depending on the radionuclide and source-target combination. SIGNIFICANCE: The developed kidney model and established dataset enable subregional dose assessment within the kidney for radiopharmaceutical therapy dosimetry. This capability facilitates evaluation of heterogeneous dose distributions among kidney substructures and may support optimization of administered activity in treatment planning.

articles.title: Unsupervised deep learning model for fast energy layer pre-selection of delivery-efficient proton arc therapy plan optimization of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
articles.abstract: Proton arc therapy (PAT) is an emerging and promising modality in radiotherapy, offering improved dose distribution and treatment robustness over conventional intensity-modulated proton therapy. Yet, identifying the optimal energy layer (EL) sequence remains challenging due to the high computational demand and prolonged treatment delivery time. This study proposes unsupervised deep learning for fast EL pre-selection, targeting EL switching (ELS) time and plan quality.Approach. We introduce a spot-count representation that combines structure-specific spot counts with spatial dose-influence features, organized by gantry angle and EL. A U-Net-style model, SPArc_dldp, uses this representation and water-equivalent thickness features to score candidate ELs, with training objectives based on spot counts and ELS time. We evaluated SPArc_dldp against SPArc_pso in 35 paired nasopharyngeal carcinoma cases, including nine-scenario robust optimization and evaluation.Main results. SPArc_dldp achieved a significantly higher nominal clinical target volume (CTV) conformity index (CI: 0.613±0.034 versus 0.557±0.040; p<0.001). It showed better homogeneity (HI: 0.395±0.048 versus 0.414±0.060; p=0.135). EL-selection computation took 2.218±0.022 ms for DL and 14.18±2.71 s for PSO. DL had significantly shorter ELS time (28.59±4.01 versus 72.19±5.56 s; p<0.001), but higher optic-nerve and parotid mean doses. Following robust optimization, DL had a higher CTV root-mean-square deviation dose-volume histogram area (RVH-AUC: 10.71±1.00 versus 8.69±0.73 per-fraction Gy(RBE)·%; p<0.001), indicating greater dose variation.Significance. The proposed spot-count representation supports rapid EL pre-selection for PAT planning. In this exploratory comparison, SPArc_dldp achieved higher nominal CI and shorter ELS time, alongside higher mean doses to some OARs and greater CTV dose variation.

articles.title: Physiology-adapted cardiac CT angiography during veno-arterial ECMO in neonatal and pediatric postoperative congenital heart disease: feasibility and clinical impact.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cardiac computed tomographic angiography (CCTA) provides high-resolution anatomical assessment in cases of congenital heart disease (CHD). This is crucial in patients supported by veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO), since the fundamental alteration of systemic hemodynamics and contrast transit kinetics makes conventional CT acquisition strategies unreliable. OBJECTIVE: We evaluated the feasibility, diagnostic yield, and clinical impact of a structured CCTA protocol adapted to ECMO-dependent physiology in postoperative neonatal and pediatric CHD patients. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective, single-center cohort study (2013-2022) included all consecutive postoperative neonatal and pediatric patients with CHD who underwent clinically indicated CCTA while supported by VA-ECMO subsequent to cardiac surgery. Contrast administration route and scan timing were individualized according to ECMO circuit flow characteristics and clinical indication. RESULTS: Twenty-six CCTA examinations were performed in 25 patients ranging in age from 3 days to 14.8 years (median age 133 days; median weight 5.1 kg). Contrast was administered via the arterial ECMO limb in 15 cases and intravenously with controlled ECMO flow modulation in 11. In 18 of the 26 examinations (69%), the examination revealed a pathology. CCTA provided anatomical information beyond echocardiography in 22 of 26 cases (85%) and directly informed a surgical or catheter-based intervention in 14 cases (54%), with procedural confirmation in all. No transport-related or CT-related adverse events occurred. CONCLUSION: When acquisition protocols are adapted to ECMO-dependent hemodynamics, CCTA is feasible and diagnostically consequential in neonatal and pediatric patients supported by VA-ECMO after congenital cardiac surgery. A physiology-guided strategy enables consistent vascular enhancement and frequently identifies clinically actionable findings not detected by echocardiography which can directly inform therapeutic decision-making in this critically ill population.

articles.title: Atypical presentation of congenital high airway obstruction sequence (CHAOS) masked by tracheo-esophageal fistula in a case of vertebral defects, anal atresia, cardiac defects, tracheo-esophageal fistula, renal anomalies, and limb abnormalities (VACTERL) association.
articles.abstract: We report an atypical case of congenital high airway obstruction sequence (CHAOS) masked by a tracheo-esophageal fistula in a neonate with VACTERL association. The case was unique because classical sonographic markers of CHAOS, such as hyperinflated lungs and hydrops, were absent, making antenatal diagnosis exceptionally difficult. The venting effect of the tracheo-esophageal fistula allowed for normal lung appearances until late gestation when severe polyhydramnios developed. This report highlights the important role of postmortem magnetic resonance imaging (PMMR) as a non-invasive diagnostic tool. PMMR provided definitive evidence of laryngeal atresia and complex fistulous anatomy, offering essential insights into why standard resuscitation failed, supporting the family's grieving process.

articles.title: Exercise-related signal abnormality (ERSA)-associated acute thigh muscle injuries in a subset of professional soccer players.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Exercise-related signal abnormality (ERSA) is a relatively new MRI entity described in professional soccer players. We report a subset of players who sustained acute muscle injuries and ERSA lesions in the same muscle. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted from July 2024 to July 2026 to identify all MRI studies of professional soccer players with an acute thigh muscle injury and ERSA lesion in the same muscle. Anatomical site, laterality, ERSA lesion subtype and length, and acute muscle injury grade as per the British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification (BAMIC) were recorded. RESULTS: There were 18 ERSA-associated acute thigh muscle injuries in 16 soccer players (12 males, 4 females; median age 20.5 years). Affected muscles were the rectus femoris (n = 12), adductor longus (n = 5), and semitendinosus (n = 1). Type C ERSA lesions (n = 13) and BAMIC grade 2b (n = 8) muscle injuries were the most common. All acute muscle injuries were located within the ERSA lesions. No intratendinous extension was observed. Median ERSA lesion length was 21.5 cm and median acute muscle injury length was 7.0 cm. The main ERSA-associated muscle injury patterns were pre-degloving (n = 6) and myofascial (n = 6) injuries of the rectus femoris and distal myotendinous junction injuries of the adductor longus (n = 4). CONCLUSION: We describe a new muscle injury pattern, termed ERSA-associated acute thigh muscle injuries, in a cohort of professional soccer players. Distinct injury patterns were observed in the rectus femoris and adductor longus.

articles.title: Preoperative prediction of Ki-67 expression in hepatocellular carcinoma using multi-sequence MRI radiomics: a non-contrast approach integrating T2-weighted, diffusion-weighted, and apparent diffusion coefficient imaging.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ki-67 is a key immunohistochemical marker of tumor proliferative activity in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC); however, non-invasive assessment of Ki-67 status before surgery remains an unmet clinical need. This study aimed to develop and internally validate multi-sequence magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) radiomics models based exclusively on non-contrast sequences for preoperative prediction of Ki-67 expression. METHODS: This retrospective study included 91 patients with 97 pathologically confirmed HCC lesions ( high Ki-67, ≥ 10%, n = 55; low Ki-67, < 10%, n = 42). Three-dimensional volumes of interest were manually segmented on T2-weighted imaging ( T2WI), diffusion-weighted imaging ( DWI), and apparent diffusion coefficient ( ADC) maps, and 5055 radiomic features ( approximately 1684 per sequence) were extracted were extracted from the three sequences. After feature selection with Pearson correlation coefficient filtering and the Kruskal-Wallis test, three multilayer perceptron ( MLP) models were constructed: Model-T ( T2WI), Model-D ( DWI + ADC), and Model-M ( combined T2WI, DWI, and ADC). The models were developed with five-fold cross-validation in the training cohort and were evaluated in a held-out testing cohort. This was a single-center retrospective study, and validation was internal only. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve ( AUC), sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy. RESULTS: No significant differences in clinical characteristics were observed between the high and low Ki-67 groups. In the training cohort, the apparent (resubstitution) AUCs of Model-T, Model-D, and Model-M were 0.715, 0.823, and 0.860, respectively (representing model fit rather than cross-validated performance). In the held-out testing cohort, the corresponding AUCs were 0.707, 0.692, and 0.716. In the testing cohort, Model-M achieved a sensitivity of 68.8%, a specificity of 53.8%, and an accuracy of 62.1%, whereas Model-D showed the most balanced performance (sensitivity, 68.8%; specificity, 76.9%; accuracy, 72.4%). The dominant features were texture features derived predominantly from the ADC sequence. The cross-validated training AUCs were considerably lower (range, 0.522-0.585). CONCLUSIONS: In this single-center, internally validated study, non-contrast multi-sequence MRI radiomics models integrating T2WI, DWI, and ADC showed moderate discrimination of Ki-67 expression in HCC. The contrast-free strategy is potentially applicable to patients with contraindications to gadolinium and warrants external validation; These findings represent internal validation only and require confirmation in external, preferably prospective multicenter, cohorts before any clinical application can be considered.

articles.title: MRI Assessment of Baseline White Matter Microstructure and Its Relationship With the Onset and Trajectory of Cancer-Related Cognitive Impairment in Breast Cancer Patients.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: White matter microstructure may be affected by cancer and its treatment, yet its association with subsequent cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI) remains unclear. PURPOSE: To investigate whether baseline white matter diffusion metrics are associated with the time to CRCI onset and longitudinal cognitive trajectories. STUDY TYPE: Prospective longitudinal study. POPULATION: A total of 230 female patients (49.4 ± 8.6 years) with histopathologically confirmed breast cancer (50 Stage II, 180 Stage III) with planned neoadjuvant chemotherapy before surgery. FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: A 3 T, multi-shell SE-EPI DWI. ASSESSMENT: Diffusion MRI was performed before chemotherapy (baseline). Neuropsychological assessments were carried out at baseline, after the first cycle of chemotherapy, after completion of chemotherapy but before surgery, and at 2-4 years after surgery. Diffusion tensor metrics (mean, radial, and axial diffusivity [MD, RD, and AD]), diffusion kurtosis metrics (axial and radial kurtosis [AK and RK]), and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging metrics (orientation dispersion index [ODI], neurite density index [NDI]) were extracted from 25 white matter tracts, capturing both mean values and peak width. STATISTICAL TESTS: Cox regression and linear mixed-effects models assessed associations with time to CRCI onset and cognitive trajectories, respectively. A p value < 0.05 was considered significant. RESULTS: Higher ODI (anterior limb of the internal capsule [ALIC]: HR = 1.28), lower AD (ALIC: HR = 0.72, external capsule [EC]: HR = 0.73, superior fronto-occipital fasciculus [SFO]: HR = 0.70), and greater peak width of AK (ALIC: HR = 1.29, EC: HR = 1.24, genu of the corpus callosum [GCC]: HR = 1.32) were associated with earlier CRCI onset. Lower FA, RK, and MK (β = 0.13 to 0.27 × 10-3), higher MD, RD, ODI, and ISOVF (β = -0.23 to -0.13 × 10-3), and higher peak width metrics (β = -0.34 to -0.13 × 10-3) were associated with poorer longitudinal cognitive trajectories. CONCLUSIONS: Pretreatment white matter microstructure may help identify patients at greater risk of CRCI and poorer cognitive trajectories. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 3.

articles.title: White Matter and Normal-Appearing White Matter in Low-Disability Patients With Multiple Sclerosis: A Diffusion Tensor MRI Study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) is sensitive to white matter (WM) microstructural alterations in multiple sclerosis (MS), but duration-defined "early MS" cohorts may be clinically heterogeneous. PURPOSE: To investigate diffusion alterations in WM and normal-appearing white matter (NAWM) in low-disability MS versus healthy controls (HC). STUDY TYPE: Retrospective cross-sectional case-control study. POPULATION: 20 patients with MS (Expanded Disability Status Scale ≤ 3.5; ambulatory without assistance) and 20 age- and sex-matched HC. SEQUENCE: 3.0 T; 3D T1-weighted and FLAIR sequences and a single-shot spin-echo echo-planar sequence with 60 diffusion directions (b = 1000 s/mm2) and nine b0 volumes. ASSESSMENT: Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS) assessed fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AD), radial diffusivity (RD), and mean diffusivity (MD) in conventional WM and lesion-masked NAWM. DeepLesionBrain (volBrain) automatically segmented WM lesions; a neuroradiologist with 10 years of experience reviewed and corrected segmentations when necessary. STATISTICAL TEST: FMRIB Software Library (FSL) randomize using 10,000 permutations, threshold-free cluster enhancement, and family-wise error correction (p < 0.01). Permutation Analysis of Linear Models (PALM) used two-sided inference and FWE correction across diffusion metrics and directions.
